paragraphs: Learning to negotiate involves two linked difficulties: deciding when to try unfamiliar actions and handling a large number of possible offers. This paper brings both into a contextual combinatorial bandit formulation. Context lets decisions depend on the situation, while the combinatorial structure represents actions assembled from multiple choices.

The resulting method, NegUCB, addresses negotiation settings with partial observations and complex rewards. It is designed for full-bandit feedback, where feedback concerns the overall chosen action rather than separate rewards for its components. The formulation does not constrain the reward functions, allowing the method to accommodate varied ways of assessing negotiation outcomes.

Under assumptions described as mild, the authors establish a sublinear upper bound on regret. This means the bound on accumulated performance loss grows more slowly than the number of decisions, rather than maintaining a constant loss per decision. Experiments on three negotiation tasks report superior performance, supporting the usefulness of combining contextual learning with a structured treatment of large action spaces.
icml-2024-a-contextual-combinatorial-ban.tldr: NegUCB frames negotiation as a contextual combinatorial bandit problem, with a conditional sublinear regret guarantee and favorable results on three tasks.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can be difficult to estimate when inclusion in an observational dataset depends on both treatment and outcome. The selected records then differ systematically from the population researchers want to understand. This paper treats that collider bias as a distribution shift between two environments: people whose records are observed and people whose records are missing.

The proposed Coupled Counterfactual Generative Adversarial Model, C²GAM, also uses a small representative dataset covering the target population. Those representative records lack labels identifying their environment. The model therefore tackles two connected reconstruction tasks: generating samples from the missing environment and generating environment labels for the representative data.

The generated missing samples are combined with the original observations before estimating treatment effects. This makes C²GAM a component that can support existing estimators, rather than requiring every estimator to solve the selection problem itself. Experiments on synthetic and real data report significant improvements when the component is added. The approach specifically relies on access to the small representative dataset alongside the selected observations.
icml-2024-a-generative-approach-for-trea.tldr: C²GAM uses representative population data to generate missing samples and improve treatment-effect estimation under collider bias.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for mathematical expressions that fit observed data. Its appeal is that the result is an explicit expression describing a relationship. The paper focuses on difficulties faced by deep generative approaches: searching among many possible expressions, learning constants, handling more input variables, and transferring effectively to unseen problems.

DySymNet changes the object being explored during that search. It considers symbolic networks with different structures and uses reinforcement learning to guide their exploration. The candidate networks are then optimized to identify expressions that fit the data better. This connects the choice of mathematical structure with the process of improving its fit to observations.

The authors evaluate DySymNet on public benchmarks with relatively few variables and on SRBench problems with more variables. They report clear advantages over several representative baseline models across these numerical experiments. Those findings support the proposed network-based search strategy across the tested problem sizes. The contribution is a way to organize expression discovery around adaptable symbolic structures, addressing the search difficulties that motivate the work.
icml-2024-a-neural-guided-dynamic-symbol.tldr: DySymNet uses reinforcement learning to explore and optimize symbolic network structures for discovering mathematical expressions from data.

paragraphs: A backdoor poisoning attack aims to make a trained network behave normally on clean inputs but produce an attacker-selected label when a trigger appears. This combination makes the phenomenon especially important to understand: accurate predictions on ordinary data can coexist with a specific, deliberately induced failure in the same model.

The paper investigates why such attacks can work through a detailed analysis of a two-layer convolutional neural network. It studies a dirty-label attack, centering the analysis on poisoned training data and the resulting model behavior. The main contribution is theoretical insight into attack effectiveness within this particular network and attack setting.

Experiments on two real-world datasets validate the theoretical findings. The work therefore connects an analytical account of backdoor learning with observed behavior on data. Its stated theoretical scope is the two-layer convolutional setting under the chosen attack. The significance is an explanation of effectiveness in that setting, helping clarify how targeted trigger behavior can emerge alongside accurate predictions for clean inputs.
icml-2024-a-theoretical-analysis-of-back.tldr: The paper theoretically analyzes dirty-label backdoor attacks in a two-layer convolutional network and validates its findings on two real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Zero-shot semantic segmentation uses language to help assign image regions to classes, including novel classes. Existing CLIP-based methods largely align text representations with visual features from the final layer. This paper argues that intermediate layers contain useful object detail, but finds that simply combining features across layers weakens performance on novel classes.

The difficulty is that features from different depths differ substantially, making a combined representation hard to align with text. Cascade-CLIP introduces independent decoders that align visual features at multiple levels with text embeddings in a cascade. This gives the different layers their own alignment components while bringing their information into the segmentation framework.

The authors describe the framework as flexible enough to apply to existing zero-shot segmentation methods. Experiments report superior zero-shot performance on COCO-Stuff, Pascal-VOC, and Pascal-Context. The central lesson from the approach is that access to more visual detail is not sufficient by itself: the method of aligning that detail with language matters for retaining the ability to recognize novel classes.
icml-2024-cascade-clip-cascaded-vision-l.tldr: Cascade-CLIP aligns visual features from multiple layers with text through separate cascaded decoders, improving zero-shot segmentation in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Code gives a language model a structured way to organize reasoning and perform precise calculations through an interpreter. However, some tasks combine computation with judgments that are difficult to implement as ordinary functions. Counting sarcastic passages, for example, requires both semantic interpretation and an exact count of the resulting decisions.

Chain of Code lets the model express semantic steps as flexible pseudocode within a program. When the interpreter encounters undefined behavior, it hands that step to a language model that simulates the expected output. The system can therefore combine executable operations with model-generated judgments while retaining the program structure linking those steps.

Experiments report that Chain of Code outperforms Chain of Thought and other baselines across several benchmarks. On BIG-Bench Hard, it reaches 84%, with a reported gain of 12% over Chain of Thought. These findings support using code-driven reasoning for questions that mix semantic and computational demands. The key contribution is the handoff between actual execution and language-model emulation within the same reasoning process.
icml-2024-chain-of-code-reasoning-with-a.tldr: Chain of Code combines interpreter execution with language-model emulation of semantic steps, improving reasoning across the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to evaluate a policy using both experimental and historical records. Its central setting has an experiment with two arms and a historical dataset containing only the control arm. The question is how to combine estimates from these sources while accounting for the possibility that rewards differ across them.

The proposed methods first construct policy-value estimators from the available sources, then combine them linearly. The combination weights are optimized to minimize mean squared error, connecting the amount of influence each estimate receives to the accuracy of the final result. The authors also apply a pessimistic principle to improve robustness and extend the methods to sequential decisions.

The theoretical analysis provides finite-sample bounds on mean squared error and establishes oracle, efficiency, and robustness properties across a broad range of reward shifts. Numerical experiments and analyses based on ridesharing-company data report superior performance. Together, these contributions provide an approach to data integration in which the weighting of separate estimates is explicitly tied to estimation error and robustness.
icml-2024-combining-experimental-and-his.tldr: The paper combines experimental and historical policy-value estimates using error-optimized weights and pessimistic adjustments for robustness.

paragraphs: Concentration inequalities describe how much random quantities can deviate from their typical values. They are important tools for understanding learning algorithms, but familiar bounded-difference results impose restrictions that do not directly accommodate unbounded fluctuations. This paper develops counterparts for general functions of independent random variables with heavy-tailed distributions.

The framework applies across heavy-tailed distributions with finite variance. That variance condition and the independence of the input variables define important parts of its stated scope. The authors illustrate the results using sub-exponential, sub-Weibull, and polynomially decaying tails, showing how the framework addresses several different forms of tail behavior.

The paper then applies the inequalities to vector-valued concentration, Rademacher complexity, and algorithmic stability. These applications extend existing statistical learning results to heavy-tailed settings down to the finite-variance requirement. The contribution is therefore both a general probabilistic tool and a route for adapting established learning-theory analyses when observations can have large, unbounded fluctuations. The stated reach concerns finite-variance distributions, including the heavier polynomial-tail examples considered.
icml-2024-concentration-inequalities-for.tldr: The paper extends bounded-difference-style concentration tools to functions of independent heavy-tailed variables with finite variance.

paragraphs: Decision-making algorithms often develop separately for single agents, cooperating teams, competitors, and mixtures of cooperation and competition. Moving between these settings changes the number of agents, their relationships, and what counts as a good solution. This paper makes a preliminary attempt to handle those differences within a shared algorithmic framework.

The first component, generalized mirror descent, uses multiple historical policies and accommodates a broader class of Bregman divergences. Configurable mirror descent adds a meta-controller that adjusts this method's hyperparameters dynamically according to the evaluation measures. The framework therefore makes adaptation to the chosen performance criterion part of the decision-making procedure.

The authors also introduce GameBench, a collection of 15 games spanning the different categories, to support evaluation across settings. Experiments find competitive or better outcomes relative to baselines and demonstrate the ability to explore different dimensions of decision making. These are empirical results supporting a preliminary unification effort. The work joins a broader optimization method, dynamic configuration, and a cross-category benchmark in one proposal.
icml-2024-configurable-mirror-descent-to.tldr: Configurable mirror descent dynamically adapts a generalized policy-update method and shows competitive results across several categories of decision making.

paragraphs: Fourier phase retrieval has an ambiguity problem: the measurements can admit equivalent solutions rather than a single absolutely unique answer. For color images, this becomes especially troublesome when each channel is reconstructed separately. Individual channel reconstructions can satisfy the retrieval problem while failing to share the orientation needed for a coherent color image.

The paper considers iterative reconstruction methods such as Relaxed Averaged Alternating Reflections. Their channel-by-channel outputs are not automatically aligned, so combining them can produce an image far from the intended color-image solution. DiffFPR integrates a diffusion model into the iterative reconstruction engine and penalizes mismatches between image channels.

The diffusion model supplies a strong prior for color images, bringing information about the joint image into a process otherwise vulnerable to separate channel ambiguities. Experiments validate the resulting algorithm for oversampled Fourier phase retrieval. The approach addresses the practical consequences of equivalent solutions through channel coordination and an image prior; the underlying lack of absolute uniqueness remains part of the problem the paper sets out to tackle.
icml-2024-difffpr-diffusion-prior-for-ov.tldr: DiffFPR combines iterative Fourier phase retrieval with a diffusion prior to address mismatches between reconstructed color channels.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning depends heavily on the trajectories already present in its dataset. When few of those trajectories are optimal, an agent faces the challenge of learning how to reach high-reward regions from less successful behavior. Useful segments may exist in the data without the connecting transitions needed to form a strong complete trajectory.

DiffStitch addresses this problem through diffusion-based data augmentation. It generates transitions that stitch different trajectories together, linking low-reward trajectories to high-reward ones. The paper describes these connections as forming globally optimal trajectories. The augmentation directly targets the difficulty of learning trajectory stitching from a dataset with limited optimal examples.

Experiments on D4RL datasets report substantial performance improvements across several approaches: the one-step method IQL, the imitation-learning method TD3+BC, and the trajectory-optimization method DT. These results support the pipeline's usefulness across different offline learning methodologies. Its central contribution is to improve the training data by generating connections between existing trajectories, making routes toward high-reward behavior more available to the learning algorithm.
icml-2024-diffstitch-boosting-offline-re.tldr: DiffStitch generates transitions connecting low- and high-reward trajectories, improving several offline reinforcement-learning methods in D4RL experiments.

paragraphs: When some classes have few training examples, a model may struggle to learn features that generalize for them. This paper uses a large pretrained teacher to help fill that information gap. It argues that conventional knowledge distillation misses an important part of the teacher's knowledge when transferring predictions to a student.

Standard distillation transfers the distribution of labels for a given input. Class-Conditional Knowledge Distillation, or CCKD, instead enables the student to learn the teacher's distribution of inputs conditioned on a class during distillation. This shifts attention toward the information associated with each class, which the paper identifies as crucial for generalization on imbalanced data.

The augmented version, ACCKD, adds distillation on a class-balanced dataset constructed through data mixing and feature imitation across the full dataset. These components combine balanced distillation with broader feature learning. Experiments on multiple imbalanced datasets report an average accuracy improvement of 7.4%. The findings support transferring class-conditional knowledge from pretrained teachers as a way to improve learning when minority-class information is scarce.
icml-2024-enhancing-class-imbalanced-lea.tldr: CCKD transfers class-conditional teacher knowledge to improve imbalanced learning, with an augmented version adding balanced data mixing and feature imitation.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization can reduce the memory and computation required by large language models. Choosing how to apply it also requires understanding what happens to model performance across different uses. This paper conducts a broad evaluation intended to support that choice, examining quantization of weights, activations, and the key-value cache.

The evaluation covers 11 model families, with model sizes ranging from 125 million to 180 billion parameters. It spans five task categories: basic natural-language processing, emergent abilities, trustworthiness, dialogue, and long-context tasks. This breadth makes different aspects of model behavior part of the assessment, alongside the efficiency motivation for compression.

The authors also evaluate state-of-the-art quantization methods to assess their applicability. They use the experimental results to summarize quantization effects, develop recommendations, and identify future research directions. The contribution is a systematic evaluation spanning model families, sizes, quantized components, and task types. It provides an empirical basis for considering performance requirements across diverse scenarios when selecting a quantization technique.
icml-2024-evaluating-quantized-large-lan.tldr: This study evaluates post-training quantization across 11 model families, three model components, and five task categories to inform method selection.

paragraphs: Explanations are intended to help people trust predictions from graph neural networks. This paper examines whether those explanations remain stable when an adversary makes small changes to the graph structure. Its central finding is that a model can continue predicting correctly while an explanation changes drastically under the perturbed graph.

The authors formulate an attack setting that restricts both the adversary's knowledge of the explainer and the number of permitted structural changes. They then develop two attack methods, one based on a loss and another based on deduction. The target is the explanation produced for the graph, with correct prediction retained in the demonstrated behavior.

Evaluations across multiple GNN explainers show fragility under these attacks. The results separate two properties that can otherwise appear closely linked: correctness of a prediction and robustness of its explanation. A stable or correct model output does not, in these experiments, ensure a stable account of why that output was produced. The restricted threat model makes that distinction relevant even when an adversary has limited information and modification capacity.
icml-2024-graph-neural-network-explanati.tldr: Small adversarial graph changes can drastically alter GNN explanations while preserving correct predictions, even under restricted attack capabilities.

paragraphs: ProtoPNet classifies images using parts intended to provide visually understandable evidence for its decisions. However, a visible image part is not necessarily meaningful to a person. The model can learn to rely on parts that make its classification display interpretable at a visual level without offering a semantically useful explanation.

The R3 framework corrects a pretrained model through reward reweighing, reselection, and retraining. Its first two stages learn a reward model from collected human feedback and align the prototypes with human preferences. This introduces an explicit human signal about which visual evidence should serve as a meaningful basis for classification.

The final stage retrains the original model's base features and classifier layer so they fit the updated prototypes. The authors describe these corrective updates as offline and efficient, and report consistent improvements in both interpretability and predictive accuracy for ProtoPNet and its variants. The findings support treating prototype quality and the surrounding classifier as connected: changing the explanatory parts is followed by realigning the model that uses them.
icml-2024-improving-prototypical-visual-.tldr: R3 uses human feedback to revise visual prototypes and retrain their supporting model, improving reported interpretability and classification accuracy.

paragraphs: In cooperative reinforcement learning, sparse rewards make it difficult for agents to discover useful behavior. Giving the whole team an additional exploration reward can help, but creates another problem: determining which individual agent contributed to the useful exploration. ICES addresses that credit-assignment difficulty by assessing each agent's contribution from a global perspective.

During centralized training, ICES uses global transition information and Bayesian surprise to construct exploration guidance. This guidance encourages individual agents toward actions that substantially influence transitions in the global latent state. The exploration scaffolds are used only during training, making their role specifically to shape how agents discover consequential behavior.

ICES also separates exploration policies from exploitation policies. That separation allows exploration to use privileged global information during training. Experiments on sparse-reward cooperative tasks, including Google Research Football and the StarCraft Multi-agent Challenge, report better exploration than the baselines. The contribution connects team-level information with individual exploration incentives, addressing the difficulty of sharing a global exploration signal among agents with different contributions.
icml-2024-individual-contributions-as-in.tldr: ICES uses global training information to reward individual contributions to exploration, improving results on sparse-reward cooperative benchmarks.

paragraphs: Visual tracking from an unmanned aerial vehicle requires fast processing on devices with limited computational capacity. Transformer-based trackers have improved tracking, but their speed can restrict practical use in this setting. AVTrack addresses that problem through adaptive computation, selecting which transformer blocks to activate during tracking.

Its Activation Module dynamically engages relevant model components to improve inference efficiency while sacrificing relatively little tracking performance. The paper also tackles a separate difficulty common in UAV footage: extreme changes in viewing angle. It learns view-invariant representations through mutual information maximization, aiming to keep the representation useful as the object's appearance changes with viewpoint.

Experiments on five tracking benchmarks support the effectiveness and versatility of the approach, and the authors report state-of-the-art tracking performance. The two components address complementary requirements of the application: selective computation supports real-time operation, while representation learning addresses viewpoint changes. The efficiency claim is explicitly qualified by a small tracking-performance compromise, making the contribution an adaptive balance between computational demand and tracking quality.
icml-2024-learning-adaptive-and-view-inv.tldr: AVTrack selectively activates transformer blocks and learns viewpoint-resistant representations to support efficient real-time UAV tracking.

paragraphs: Collider bias can make treatment-effect estimation unreliable when the observed sample is selected in a way that distorts the relevant relationships. A shadow variable can help identify treatment effects in this setting. It must relate to the outcome while remaining independent of sample selection after conditioning on the other observed variables.

Finding a variable with those properties ordinarily requires domain expertise. This paper instead proposes learning shadow-variable representations automatically from observational data without prior knowledge. A tester performs hypothesis testing during representation learning. The procedure alternates between generating representations and checking the shadow-variable assumptions, continuing until a representation passes the test.

The learned representations then support a new treatment-effect estimator designed to address collider bias. Experiments report that the proposed methods outperform existing treatment-effect estimation methods in the studied collider-bias settings. The distinctive contribution is the integration of representation learning with explicit checks of the required assumptions. Those assumptions remain central to the approach, with hypothesis testing providing the stated mechanism for assessing candidate representations.
icml-2024-learning-shadow-variable-repre.tldr: The paper learns and tests shadow-variable representations from observational data to support treatment-effect estimation under collider bias.

paragraphs: Compressing large language models can reduce their substantial parameter and resource requirements. LoRAP starts from an observation that different transformer sublayers have different structures: multi-head self-attention exhibits noticeable low-rank structure, while the feed-forward network does not. The method therefore chooses a different structured compression technique for each kind of sublayer.

For attention, LoRAP uses singular value decomposition weighted by input activations. It also assigns different parameter budgets to weight matrices according to differences in their low-rank properties. For feed-forward networks, it uses structured channel pruning without gradients. The method additionally retains the 1% of parameters described as least important, which the authors find nevertheless play a vital role in performance.

Evaluations using zero-shot perplexity and zero-shot classification report better results than previous structured compression methods at multiple compression ratios. These findings support matching compression to the internal properties of model components. The contribution combines low-rank approximation and pruning within one method, with both sublayer-level choices and matrix-specific parameter allocation shaping how the model is compressed.
icml-2024-lorap-transformer-sub-layers-d.tldr: LoRAP combines low-rank attention compression with feed-forward channel pruning, exploiting differences between transformer sublayers.

paragraphs: Latent diffusion models can learn new concepts by fine-tuning on only a few images, raising privacy concerns for personal images available online. Existing protective methods often assume that the defender and the party exploiting the images use exactly matching text prompts. This paper investigates what happens when that assumption fails.

The authors empirically show that differences between those prompts can substantially weaken prior defenses. They then examine the visual encoder, whose operation is independent of text prompts, and study how manipulating it affects few-shot fine-tuning. That investigation motivates Prompt-Independent Defense, or PID, which bases protection on this prompt-independent part of the model.

The paper reports that PID provides strong standalone privacy protection while requiring significantly less computation. Its central contribution is to identify prompt matching as a consequential assumption and develop a defense around a component that does not depend on the prompt. The reported findings support this design as a step toward more reliable protection of image data against misuse through latent diffusion model fine-tuning.
icml-2024-pid-prompt-independent-data-pr.tldr: PID targets the prompt-independent visual encoder to protect images from latent diffusion fine-tuning without relying on matching text prompts.

paragraphs: Gaussian process latent variable models learn lower-dimensional representations without supervision. They can collapse into vague representations that fail to capture the structure of the data. This paper examines two contributing problems: insufficiently flexible kernels and poorly chosen projection noise. It first analyzes the influence of projection variance theoretically through a linear version of the model.

The proposed advisedRFLVM combines a spectral mixture kernel with a differentiable random Fourier feature approximation. The kernel addresses flexibility, while the approximation supports computational scalability and efficiency. Within variational inference, standard automatic differentiation tools learn the kernel hyperparameters, projection variance, and latent representations, bringing these quantities into the same learning framework.

Across diverse datasets, the authors report consistently better latent representations and missing-data imputation than competing models, including variational autoencoders and other GPLVM variants. These findings connect the model-design changes to both representation quality and a task that uses those representations. The contribution pairs a theoretical investigation of projection variance with a scalable, more flexible model intended to address the identified sources of collapse.
icml-2024-preventing-model-collapse-in-g.tldr: advisedRFLVM combines a flexible kernel and differentiable approximation to address latent-representation collapse and improve reported missing-data imputation.

paragraphs: Adaptive experiments must balance learning about treatment effects with providing beneficial treatments to participants. In clinical settings, they must also protect sensitive records. This paper studies that balance using contextual bandits, with conditional average treatment-effect estimation representing the learning objective and regret measuring the loss of participant welfare.

The authors establish matching upper and lower bounds for the resulting multi-objective problem. They use Pareto optimality to characterize optimal tradeoffs, describing the boundary at which improving one objective requires a sacrifice in another. This makes estimation quality and treatment allocation part of one theoretical analysis rather than treating either objective in isolation.

The paper then proposes differentially private algorithms that still match the lower bound, supporting its characterization of privacy as almost free in the analyzed setting. It also derives asymptotic normality for the estimator, providing a basis for statistical inference and hypothesis testing. Together, these results connect privacy-preserving allocation with optimal welfare–estimation tradeoffs and the inferential properties needed to interpret estimated treatment effects.
icml-2024-privacy-preserving-adaptive-ex.tldr: The paper characterizes welfare–estimation tradeoffs in adaptive experiments and develops differentially private algorithms that match the theoretical lower bound.

paragraphs: Sparse neural networks reduce computational and memory demands, but many training methods produce only one subnetwork with a fixed sparsity pattern and ratio. That restricts adaptation to different hardware or resource budgets. Sparse Cocktail broadens joint subnetwork training to include multiple patterns and multiple ratios within the same framework.

The method alternates training among subnetworks with different sparsity patterns while gradually increasing sparsity ratios across patterns. A unified mask-generation process and Dense Pivot Co-training coordinate the parameters shared by those subnetworks. These components are intended to prevent training for one pattern from canceling the performance of another pattern that uses overlapping parameters.

At inference, the trained collection supports switching between sparsity patterns and ratios according to available hardware. Experiments on image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation illustrate the framework's effectiveness and flexibility. The contribution expands the range of deployment choices supported by sparse co-training: resource adaptation can involve both how much of the network is retained and the structural pattern of what remains.
icml-2024-sparse-cocktail-every-sparse-p.tldr: Sparse Cocktail jointly trains subnetworks with multiple sparsity patterns and ratios so deployment can adapt to available hardware.

paragraphs: Research on reducing harmful uses of language models needs evaluations that researchers can access and reuse. The paper identifies private evaluations and narrow scenario coverage as obstacles to that work. It introduces WMDP, a public benchmark of 3,668 multiple-choice questions spanning biosecurity, cybersecurity, and chemical security.

The questions are designed as a proxy for hazardous knowledge. Alongside the benchmark, the authors develop RMU, an unlearning method that operates by controlling model representations. The pairing provides both a measurement target and a method intended to reduce a model's performance on that target while preserving useful capabilities.

The authors report that RMU lowers performance on WMDP while retaining general capabilities in areas including biology and computer science. This suggests that unlearning may offer a concrete route toward reducing malicious use. The proxy distinction matters when interpreting the result: the demonstrated change concerns hazardous-knowledge benchmark performance, and the paper presents reduced malicious use as a possibility supported by those findings. Public benchmark and code releases make this research direction accessible for further study.
icml-2024-the-wmdp-benchmark-measuring-a.tldr: WMDP provides a public hazardous-knowledge proxy benchmark, while RMU reduces benchmark performance and preserves reported general capabilities.

paragraphs: Skills combine behavior across time and are intended to make hierarchical reinforcement learning more effective. This paper asks which properties of an environment determine whether they help. Its characterization focuses on deterministic skills in deterministic environments with sparse rewards and finite action spaces, giving the analysis a specific mathematical setting.

The authors show theoretically and empirically that the performance gain from skills is worse when solutions to states are less compressible. This connects usefulness to how compactly solution behavior can be represented. The finding gives a more precise criterion for reasoning about skill utility than the general intuition that temporally extended behavior should simplify learning.

Further theoretical results suggest that skills help exploration more than learning from already collected experience. They also suggest that insufficiently expressive skills, including macroactions, may reduce performance. These conclusions distinguish the benefits of discovering experience from those of learning from it, while making skill expressiveness consequential. The findings are intended to guide automatic skill discovery and decisions about when and how to use skills within the analyzed setting.
icml-2024-when-do-skills-help-reinforcem.tldr: In the analyzed deterministic setting, skills yield smaller gains when solutions are less compressible, and unexpressive skills may hurt performance.
